title: Why HR departments run with AI agents will still require humans
excerpt: Despite flashy headlines, companies are not wiping out their HR departments — not even to implement AI, experts told HR Dive.
content_html:
Kathryn Moody

Fri, August 28, 2026 at 3:24 AM MST 5 min read

This story was originally published on HR Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily HR Dive newsletter.

As more companies expect artificial intelligence tool use to go beyond simple tasks, HR departments continue to mull how AI agents will be implemented — and who might lose their positions because of them.

A report from The Josh Bersin Co. released in June projected that, by 2030, HR departments could see their head counts reduced somewhere between 30% to 50% due to the HR capabilities that AI agents could undertake. 

But the inherent complexity of HR complicates these matters, the report noted. The HR function includes more than 250 specialized roles and 400 skills, the company said — and while that paves the way for usage of more than 100 types of AI agents, "agent sprawl" is not the goal. An entirely new HR architecture is.

And that architecture will require humans.

While CEOs have pressured their companies to use AI to drive productivity, including to perhaps cut head count, those cuts have not really come about, said Eser Rizaoglu, VP analyst in the Gartner HR Practice. Layoffs that have occurred have largely been due to the inflated head counts propagated by hiring during the pandemic, Rizaoglu noted.

Even as AI agents proliferate, HR will still lead strategy, Josh Bersin told HR Dive. But the real truth may be even simpler: Someone has to instruct and manage the AI agents for them to be effective in the first place, and most companies are still figuring out how that looks in practice.

Where will jobs go?

Despite flashy headlines, companies are not wiping out their HR departments, Bersin said. Aggregate job postings for HR roles are flat, he noted, which indicates a "rebalancing" rather than a recession of the profession.

AI agents are predicted to take on tasks that are easy to automate, such as helping a worker find information on their pay stub or adjusting their payroll to accommodate tax changes — operational work that many HR people don't particularly enjoy, he said.

Instead, as AI agents take on administratively heavy jobs that once may have required quite a few people, HR professionals can spend time doing "more valuable things," Bersin said, such as discovering where the "actual problems" are in a process or in an employee experience.

Such a shift may particularly change junior or entry-level jobs, Rizaoglu said, but in HR, AI agent models will most likely hew to a "human in the loop" approach that keeps a person available to check outputs and maintain the system when a machine inevitably breaks.
